. It briefly discusses the 50-year historic debate about whether environment should be a security issue—and if so, how. It then elucidates some of the most important domestic (U.S.) and international public policy and public management implications of environmental security that are becoming evident, or increasingly feared, including cascading, threat-multiplying security risk scenarios. It reviews some of what is currently known about the science of human-caused climate disruption and the complex interaction with environmental degradation from population growth and nonrenewable resource exploitation.

This is not a novel observation, but for many years evidence has gradually accumulated indicating a significant risk of not only incremental, but abrupt, catastrophic climate changes (NRC, 2013; Schwartz & Randall, 2003; Showstack, 2013). Scientific research increasingly indicates that the time grows more urgent than most analysts and scholars had, until recently, assumed for mitigating and adapting to changing, destructive human patterns (Durack, Gleckler, Landerer, & Taylor, 2014; Mann, 2014; NRC, 2013; Stanton, Shoemaker, Pearson, & AkcS akaya, 2015). and outcomes.4 Background 2014 was the hottest year ever recorded on global land and ocean surfaces at the time, and with the help of the 2015–16 El Nino (ENSO) weather pattern, 2015 was on course to be even hotter (Trenberth, 2015). It was also among the ten hottest in history—all of which had occurred in the previous 16 years, since 1998. The 2014 annually averaged global temperature was 0.69˚C (1.24˚F) above the 20th century average—and above that average for the 38th consecutive year in a row (since1977). Put differently, at least nine of the ten warmest years in the 135-year historical temperature record have occurred since 2000, and this pattern is consistent with rising average temperatures since the 1800s industrial revolution began pumping 186 Risk, Hazards & Crisis in Public Policy, 6:2 greenhouse gases, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2), into the atmosphere (NOAA, 2014a). The odds of these temperatures occurring randomly, instead of being caused primarily by manmade greenhouse gas pollution (in combination with less important natural variables), are staggering: 1 in 27 million, by one estimate (Climate Central,2015). Worsening current climate changes and evidence from modeling future outcomes further reinforces the critical importance of strengthening the analytical and institutional ties among homeland security, national strategic security, and environmental security—at various levels of theory and policy practice. This integration is necessary to maximize global mitigation and adaptation, and minimize the likely damage to human social, political, economic, and physical infrastructure systems (IPCC, 2014; NCA, 2014; NRC, 2013; World Bank, 2012).

Even though they may of may not have been exacerbated by climate change, all of those storms were predictable based on historic variability. For example, years before either Katrina or Sandy, analysts had been modeling potential disaster just like the ones that occurred, predicting that New Orleans would experience a major hurricane that could breach the levees and flood walls, but U.S. government funding for significant engineering improvements never emerged (Lin & Emanuel, 2015; PatéCornell, 2012).
